passages.passageHtml:
Saturday morning was come, and all the summer world was bright and fresh, and brimming with life. There was a song in every heart; and if the heart was young the music issued at the lips. Tom appeared on the sidewalk with a bucket of whitewash and a longhandled brush. He surveyed the fence, and all gladness left him and a deep melancholy settled down upon his spirit. Thirty yards of board fence nine feet high. Life to him seemed hollow, and existence but a burden.

He sat down on a tree-box discouraged. Jim came skipping out with a tin pail, singing. Bringing water from the town pump had always been hateful work in Tom's eyes, but now it did not strike him so. He remembered that there was company at the pump. Tom tried to trade: "Say, Jim, I'll fetch the water if you'll whitewash some." Jim refused, afraid of Aunt Polly. Tom offered a white alley marble. Jim began to waver. Tom added, "I'll show you my sore toe." Jim put down his pail and bent over the toe with interest. In another moment he was flying down the street with his pail and a tingling rear, Tom was whitewashing with vigor, and Aunt Polly was retiring from the field with a slipper in her hand and triumph in her eye.

Tom's energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon free boys would come tripping along on expeditions, and they would make fun of him for having to work. He got out his worldly wealth—bits of toys, marbles, and trash—enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy half an hour of freedom. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him.

PRIDE & PREJUDICE.

CHAPTER I.

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

"My dear Mr. Bennet," said his lady to him one day, "have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last?"

Mr. Bennet replied that he had not.

"But it is," returned she; "for Mrs. Long has just been here, and she told me all about it."

Mr. Bennet made no answer.

"Do not you want to know who has taken it?" cried his wife impatiently.

"You want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it."

This was invitation enough.

"Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says that Netherfield is taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England; that he came down on Monday in a chaise and four to see the place, and was so much delighted with it that he agreed with Mr. Morris immediately; that he is to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week."

"What is his name?"

"Bingley."

"Is he married or single?"

"Oh! single, my dear, to be sure! A single man of large fortune; four or five thousand a year. What a fine thing for our girls!"

"How so? how can it affect them?"

"My dear Mr. Bennet," replied his wife, "how can you be so tiresome! You must know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them."

"Is that his design in settling here?"

"Design! nonsense, how can you talk so! But it is very likely that he may fall in love with one of them, and therefore you must visit him as soon as he comes."

"I see no occasion for that. You and the girls may go, or you may send them by themselves, which perhaps will be still better, for as you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley might like you the best of the party."

"My dear, you flatter me. I certainly have had my share of beauty, but I do not pretend to be any thing extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown up daughters, she ought to give over thinking of her own beauty."

"In such cases, a woman has not often much beauty to think of."

"But, my dear, you must indeed go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes into the neighbourhood."

"It is more than I engage for, I assure you."

"But consider your daughters. Only think what an establishment it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, merely on that account, for in general you know they visit no new comers. Indeed you must go, for it will be impossible for us to visit him, if you do not."

"You are over scrupulous surely. I dare say Mr. Bingley will be very glad to see you; and I will send a few lines by you to assure him of my hearty consent to his marrying which ever he chuses of the girls; though I must throw in a good word for my little Lizzy."

"I desire you will do no such thing. Lizzy is not a bit better than the others; and I am sure she is not half so handsome as Jane, nor half so good humoured as Lydia. But you are always giving her the preference."

"They have none of them much to recommend them," replied he; "they are all silly and ignorant like other girls; but Lizzy has something more of quickness than her sisters."

"Mr. Bennet, how can you abuse your own children in such a way? You take delight in vexing me. You have no compassion on my poor nerves."

"You mistake me, my dear. I have a high respect for your nerves. They are my old friends. I have heard you mention them with consideration these twenty years at least."

"Ah! you do not know what I suffer."

"But I hope you will get over it, and live to see many young men of four thousand a year come into the neighbourhood."

I resisted all the way: a new thing for me, and a circumstance which greatly strengthened the bad opinion Bessie and Miss Abbot were disposed to entertain of me. The fact is, I was a trifle beside myself; or rather out of myself, as the French would say: I was conscious that a moment's mutiny had already rendered me liable to strange penalties, and, like any other rebel slave, I felt resolved, in my desperation, to go all lengths.

"Hold her arms, Miss Abbot: she's like a mad cat."

"For shame! for shame!" cried the lady's-maid. "What shocking conduct, Miss Eyre, to strike a young gentleman, your benefactress's son! Your young master."

"Master! How is he my master? Am I a servant?"

"No; you are less than a servant, for you do nothing for your keep. There, sit down, and think over your wickedness."

They had got me by this time into the apartment indicated by Mrs. Reed, and had thrust me upon a stool: my impulse was to rise from it like a spring; their two pair of hands arrested me instantly.

"If you don't sit still, you must be tied down," said Bessie. "Miss Abbot, lend me your garters; she would break mine directly."

Miss Abbot turned to divest a stout leg of the necessary ligature. This preparation for bonds, and the additional ignominy it inferred, took a little of the excitement out of me.

"Don't take them off," I cried; "I will not stir."

"You ought to be aware, Miss, that you are under obligations to Mrs. Reed: she keeps you: if she were to turn you off, you would have to go to the poorhouse."

I had nothing to say to these words: they were not new to me: my very first recollections of existence included hints of the same kind. This reproach of my dependence had become a vague singsong in my ear: very painful and crushing, but only half intelligible.

"What we tell you is for your good," added Bessie, in no harsh voice, "you should try to be useful and pleasant, then, perhaps, you would have a home here; but if you become passionate and rude, Missis will send you away, I am sure."

"Besides," said Miss Abbot, "God will punish her: He might strike her dead in the midst of her tantrums, and then where would she go? Come, Bessie, we will leave her: I wouldn't have her heart for anything. Say your prayers, Miss Eyre, when you are by yourself; for if you don't repent, something bad might be permitted to come down the chimney and fetch you away."

They went, shutting the door, and locking it behind them.

My father's family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip. So, I called myself Pip, and came to be called Pip.

I give Pirrip as my father's family name, on the authority of his tombstone and my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith. As I never saw my father or my mother, and never saw any likeness of either of them (for their days were long before the days of photographs), my first fancies regarding what they were like were unreasonably derived from their tombstones. The shape of the letters on my father's, gave me an odd idea that he was a square, stout, dark man, with curly black hair. From the character and turn of the inscription, "Also Georgiana Wife of the Above," I drew a childish conclusion that my mother was freckled and sickly. To five little stone lozenges, each about a foot and a half long, which were arranged in a neat row beside their grave, and were sacred to the memory of five little brothers of mine, who gave up trying to get a living, exceedingly early in that universal struggle, I am indebted for a belief I religiously entertained that they had all been born on their backs with their hands in their trousers-pockets, and had never taken them out in this state of existence.

Ours was the marsh country, down by the river, within, as the river wound, twenty miles of the sea. My first most vivid and broad impression of the identity of things seems to me to have been gained on a memorable raw afternoon towards evening. At such a time I found out for certain that this bleak place overgrown with nettles was the churchyard; and that Philip Pirrip, late of this parish, and also Georgiana wife of the above, were dead and buried; and that Alexander, Bartholomew, Abraham, Tobias, and Roger, infant children of the aforesaid, were also dead and buried; and that the dark flat wilderness beyond the churchyard, intersected with dikes and mounds and gates, with scattered cattle feeding on it, was the marshes; and that the low leaden line beyond was the river; and that the distant savage lair from which the wind was rushing was the sea; and that the small bundle of shivers growing afraid of it all and beginning to cry, was Pip.

"Hold your noise!" cried a terrible voice, as a man started up from among the graves at the side of the church porch. "Keep still, you little devil, or I'll cut your throat!"

A fearful man, all in coarse grey, with a great iron on his leg. A man with no hat, and with broken shoes, and with an old rag tied round his head. A man who had been soaked in water, and smothered in mud, and lamed by stones, and cut by flints, and stung by nettles, and torn by briars; who limped, and shivered, and glared, and growled; and whose teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin.

"Oh! Don't cut my throat, sir," I pleaded in terror. "Pray don't do it, sir."

"Tell us your name!" said the man. "Quick!"

"Pip, sir."

"Once more," said the man, staring at me. "Give it mouth!"

"Pip. Pip, sir."

I pointed to where our village lay, on the flat inshore among the alder-trees and pollards, a mile or more from the church.

The man, after looking at me for a moment, turned me upside down, and emptied my pockets. There was nothing in them but a piece of bread. When the church came to itself, for he was so sudden and strong that he made it go head over heels before me, and I saw the steeple under my feet, when the church came to itself, I say, I was seated on a high tombstone, trembling while he ate the bread ravenously.

The widow she cried over me, and called me a poor lost lamb, and she called me a lot of other names, too, but she never meant no harm by it. She put me in them new clothes again, and I couldn't do nothing but sweat and sweat, and feel all cramped up. Well, then, the old thing commenced again. The widow rung a bell for supper, and you had to come to time. When you got to the table you couldn't go right to eating, but you had to wait for the widow to tuck down her head and grumble a little over the victuals, though there wasn't really anything the matter with them, that is, nothing only everything was cooked by itself. In a barrel of odds and ends it is different; things get mixed up, and the juice kind of swaps around, and the things go better.

After supper she got out her book and learned me about Moses and the Bulrushers, and I was in a sweat to find out all about him; but by- and- by she let it out that Moses had been dead a considerable long time; so then I didn't care no more about him, because I don't take no stock in dead people.

Pretty soon I wanted to smoke, and asked the widow to let me. But she wouldn't. She said it was a mean practice and wasn't clean, and I must try to not do it any more. That is just the way with some people. They get down on a thing when they don't know nothing about it. Here she was a- bothering about Moses, which was no kin to her, and no use to anybody, being gone, you see, yet finding a power of fault with me for doing a thing that had some good in it. And she took snuff, too; of course that was all right, because she done it herself.

Her sister, Miss Watson, a tolerable slim old maid, with goggles on, had just come to live with her, and took a set at me now with a spelling- book. She worked me middling hard for about an hour, and then the widow made her ease up. I couldn't stood it much longer. Then for an hour it was deadly dull, and I was fidgety. Miss Watson would say, "Don't put your feet up there, Huckleberry;" and "Don't scrunch up like that, Huckleberry—set up straight;" and pretty soon she would say, "Don't gap and stretch like that, Huckleberry—why don't you try to behave?" Then she told me all about the bad place, and I said I wished I was there. She got mad then, but I didn't mean no harm. All I wanted was to go somewheres; all I wanted was a change, I warn't particular. She said it was wicked to say what I said; said she wouldn't say it for the whole world; she was going to live so as to go to the good place. Well, I couldn't see no set down again, a- shaking all over, and got out my pipe for a smoke; for the house was all as still as death now, and so the widow wouldn't know. Well, after a long time I heard the clock away off in the town go boom- boom- boom—twelve licks; and all still again—stiller than ever. Pretty soon I heard a twig snap down in the dark amongst the trees—something was a stirring. I set still and listened. Directly I could just barely hear a "me- yow! me- yow!" down there. That was good! Says I, "me- yow! me- yow!" as soft as I could, and then I put out the light and scrambled out of the window on to the shed. Then I slipped down to the ground and crawled in among the trees, and, sure enough, there was Tom Sawyer waiting for me.

questions.questionHtml: What does Tom's offer to show Jim his "sore toe" reveal about Tom's understanding of human behavior, based only on events in the passage?

options.A: Tom believes that physical pain is the only reliable way to control others, so he threatens to inflict pain if Jim refuses.
options.B: Tom knows that curiosity and distraction can be more powerful than fear of punishment, even when material rewards have only partial effect.
options.C: Tom thinks that showing weakness makes other people feel superior and more likely to help, so he pretends to be injured to gain sympathy.
options.D: Tom assumes that all boys are primarily motivated by the promise of material rewards, and the toe is just another form of bribery.

questions.explanationHtml: Tom first offers a marble (material). Jim still fears Aunt Polly's punishment. Then Tom offers to show his sore toe - pure curiosity, no value. Jim immediately gives in. This shows Tom understands curiosity/distraction can override fear, not pain (A), sympathy (C), or only material rewards (D).

questions.questionHtml:
Place the following events in the order they occur in the passage. Which of the following sequences is correct?

Events:
A. Tom offers Jim a white alley marble.
B. Jim is sent flying down the street with a tingling rear.
C. Tom adds, "I'll show you my sore toe."
D. Aunt Polly retires from the field with a slipper in her hand and triumph in her eye.
E. Tom suggests trading: "I'll fetch the water if you'll whitewash some."

options.A: E, A, C, B, D
options.B: A, E, C, B, D
options.C: E, C, A, B, D
options.D: A, C, E, B, D

questions.explanationHtml: The correct chronological order: 1. Tom first tries to trade (E), 2. then offers a marble (A), 3. then adds the sore toe (C), 4. Jim is sent flying (B), 5. Aunt Polly leaves with slipper and triumph (D).

questions.questionHtml: At the beginning of the passage, Tom sees fetching water from the town pump as "hateful work." Later, he thinks it might not be so bad because "there was company at the pump." What does this change most clearly suggest about Tom's attitude toward work?

options.A: Tom believes that any task becomes enjoyable if it involves physical activity rather than standing still.
options.B: Tom values social interaction so highly that even unpleasant work seems tolerable when it includes the chance to be with others.
options.C: Tom has realized that fetching water is actually easier than whitewashing, so he tries to trick Jim into a worse job.
options.D: Tom only hates work when he is forced to do it alone; with company, he forgets the effort entirely.

questions.explanationHtml: The passage explicitly says fetching water "had always been hateful work" but now "did not strike him so" because he remembered there was company at the pump. Tom's shift is driven by the prospect of social contact, not physical activity (A), not a calculation of difficulty (C), and not forgetting effort (D - he still remembers it's work, but the company changes his feeling).

questions.questionHtml: Tom examines his "worldly wealth—bits of toys, marbles, and trash" and concludes it is "not half enough to buy half an hour of freedom." What does this realization most strongly imply about Tom's situation?

options.A: Tom has been saving for a long time but is poor at bargaining, so he underestimates what his items are worth.
options.B: Tom is so desperate to avoid the shame of being seen working that he would trade anything, but he lacks sufficient valuables.
options.C: Tom mistakenly believes that freedom can only be purchased, when in fact he could simply run away from the fence.
options.D: Tom's wealth is larger than he thinks, but he is too discouraged to calculate correctly.

questions.explanationHtml: Earlier, Tom fears that "free boys" will make fun of him for working. His sorrows multiply. He then checks his possessions and finds them insufficient to buy freedom. This shows his desperation to avoid public shame (social pain) outweighs his attachment to his toys. Option B captures this. A is wrong - no bargaining skill is mentioned. C is wrong - running away would bring Aunt Polly's punishment, so not real freedom. D contradicts the text.

questions.questionHtml: Based on the dialogue and the narrator's description of Mr. Bennet, what is the most likely reason he repeatedly claims he will not visit Mr. Bingley?

options.A: He believes that a father who actively pursues a wealthy stranger for his daughters might appear improper or desperate, which could harm their chances.
options.B: He sees no practical benefit from visiting because, as he points out, his wife and daughters could go without him, and a visit from them might be just as effective.
options.C: He enjoys provoking his wife's anxieties and frustrations, and his refusal is a form of private amusement rather than a serious objection.
options.D: He thinks that remaining detached from the matchmaking process allows him to later support whichever daughter actually attracts Bingley, without having shown favoritism.

questions.explanationHtml: The narrator explicitly states that Mr. Bennet has "sarcastic humour" and takes "delight in vexing" his wife. Throughout the dialogue, he refuses to visit Bingley not because he actually objects, but because he enjoys teasing Mrs. Bennet and watching her become frustrated. His later suggestion that he might send a note of consent to Bingley shows he is not truly opposed to the match - he is simply amused by his wife's anxiety.

questions.questionHtml: How does the famous opening sentence ("It is a truth universally acknowledged...") function in relation to Mrs. Bennet's subsequent dialogue and actions?

options.A: It presents a widely accepted belief about wealthy unmarried men, and the conversation then shows how Mrs. Bennet's concerns are a reasonable application of that belief.
options.B: It foreshadows that Mr. Bennet will eventually visit Mr. Bingley, because the "truth" of the sentence forces him to act in his daughters' interest.
options.C: It serves as a satirical summary of the exact mindset that Mrs. Bennet embodies - treating a wealthy single man as an automatic marriage opportunity for her daughters.
options.D: It introduces the economic reality that unmarried wealthy men are expected to marry, which explains why Mrs. Bennet feels such urgency despite her husband's resistance.

questions.explanationHtml: The opening sentence is ironic. Although it is phrased as a universal truth, it is actually a satirical observation about how society thinks. Mrs. Bennet immediately demonstrates this mindset by assuming that a wealthy single man must want a wife and that her daughters are the obvious candidates. She treats Bingley as "rightful property" of one of her daughters, exactly as the opening sentence describes. The narrator uses this irony to highlight the absurdity of such social assumptions.

questions.questionHtml: When Mr. Bennet says Lizzy has "something more of quickness than her sisters," while Mrs. Bennet praises Jane as "handsome" and Lydia as "good humoured," what inference is best supported about their differing parental values?

options.A: Mr. Bennet values intellectual sharpness and wit, whereas Mrs. Bennet values traits that are most likely to attract a husband (beauty and good humor).
options.B: Mr. Bennet prefers daughters who show independence and a playful spirit, while Mrs. Bennet favors daughters who are obedient and eager to please strangers.
options.C: Mr. Bennet believes that none of his daughters are truly exceptional, so he exaggerates Lizzy's quickness to avoid admitting they are average, while Mrs. Bennet gives a more practical ranking.
options.D: Mr. Bennet judges his daughters by how well they might manage a household after marriage, whereas Mrs. Bennet judges them by their behavior at social gatherings.

questions.explanationHtml: "Quickness" in this context refers to mental agility and intelligence. Mr. Bennet values Lizzy's sharp mind, whereas Mrs. Bennet dismisses Lizzy because she lacks the conventional beauty of Jane and the cheerful sociability of Lydia - traits that Mrs. Bennet believes are necessary to attract a husband. This contrast shows that Mr. Bennet appreciates inner qualities, whereas Mrs. Bennet focuses on outward, marriageable traits.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following conclusions about the society depicted in the passage is most strongly supported by Mrs. Bennet's sense of urgency and the fact that Sir William and Lady Lucas, who "in general... visit no new comers," are determined to visit Bingley?

options.A: Families usually avoid newcomers to protect their social reputation, but a wealthy bachelor is such a valuable prize that they will risk appearing desperate.
options.B: A newcomer's wealth directly determines how quickly local families will abandon their normal social habits, with Bingley's fortune being the main reason for the exception.
options.C: Local families are generally eager to welcome any newcomer regardless of wealth, but Mrs. Bennet misinterprets the Lucases' intentions as purely marriage-driven.
options.D: Securing a wealthy husband for a daughter is treated as an economic necessity so powerful that it overrides ordinary social caution.

questions.explanationHtml: Mrs. Bennet repeatedly emphasizes what an "establishment" (i.e., financial security and social position) a Bingley marriage would provide. The Lucases, who normally "visit no new comers," are determined to break their own rule "merely on that account" - meaning solely because of the marriage opportunity. This proves that securing a wealthy husband is treated as an economic necessity so powerful that it overrides ordinary social caution. No other conclusion is as directly supported by the text.

questions.questionHtml: When Jane asks, "Am I a servant?" and is told she is "less than a servant," what does the author most likely imply about Jane's position in the household?

options.A: Jane has no legal rights as a child dependent, so she must accept the Reeds' authority without question.
options.B: Jane is expected to be grateful for basic shelter, yet she has no real status, security, or wages.
options.C: Servants at least earn their keep through work, while Jane receives only charity and therefore has even less power.
options.D: Mrs. Reed treats Jane more harshly than the servants because Jane is not a blood relative.

questions.explanationHtml:
The passage emphasizes that Jane does "nothing for your keep" and is threatened with the poorhouse. She has no wage, no role, and no security — "less than a servant" means she is a helpless dependent, not a worker with any standing.

A is too legalistic; the passage focuses on status and gratitude, not rights. C is partially true but misses the core idea: the implication is not just about earning keep but about powerlessness. D is not directly supported; Mrs. Reed's reasoning is not explained in this passage.

questions.questionHtml: The author writes that Jane felt "like any other rebel slave" and was "resolved... to go all lengths." What does this comparison most strongly suggest about Jane's emotional state?

options.A: Jane believes that physical rebellion is the only way to make adults respect her.
options.B: Jane sees her resistance as a desperate fight for survival, not merely childish stubbornness.
options.C: Jane feels trapped between the normal rules of childhood and the harsh reality of adult authority.
options.D: Jane's resistance comes from a deep sense of injustice about how she is treated.

questions.explanationHtml:
"Rebel slave" and "go all lengths" point to a life-or-death psychological struggle. Jane is desperate, not just naughty or unfairly treated — the comparison elevates her resistance to survival-level intensity.

A is too narrow; the passage focuses on desperation, not strategy. C is plausible but too general — the slave comparison is more extreme. D is true but incomplete; the passage emphasizes desperation, not just injustice.

questions.questionHtml: Bessie says the reproach of dependence had become "a vague sing-song" in Jane's ear that was "only half intelligible." What does this description reveal about Jane's experience?

options.A: Jane has heard the same accusations so often that they blur together, yet they still cause her pain.
options.B: Jane has learned to block out hurtful words as a way of protecting herself emotionally.
options.C: The accusations confuse Jane because the adults speak in contradictions she cannot resolve.
options.D: Jane is too young to fully understand money and social status, so the threats don't fully register.

questions.explanationHtml:
"Vague sing-song" means the accusations blur from repetition, and "half intelligible" means she doesn't fully process them — yet they are still "very painful and crushing."

B is incorrect; she is not numb — the words are still painful. C is possible but not the main point; the passage emphasizes repetition, not contradiction. D is partially true but misses the emotional crushing effect.

questions.questionHtml: Miss Abbot warns that God "might strike her dead in the midst of her tantrums" and that "something bad" might come down the chimney. What is the most likely purpose of this warning?

options.A: To remind Jane that religious faith requires her to forgive the Reed family for their harsh treatment.
options.B: To frighten Jane into controlling her anger by threatening supernatural punishment.
options.C: To convince Jane that emotional self-control is morally important for her own salvation.
options.D: To explain that God watches all children and punishes those who are disobedient.

questions.explanationHtml:
The warning uses divine and supernatural threats (being struck dead, a chimney monster) to scare Jane into obedience. The goal is control through fear, not genuine moral instruction.

A is incorrect; forgiveness is not mentioned. C is tempting but too reasonable — the passage emphasizes terror, not moral teaching. D is partially true but misses the manipulative, fear-based tone; it's not about general divine justice but immediate intimidation.

questions.questionHtml: The author emphasizes that the door was locked behind Jane. What is the most likely reason for including this detail?

options.A: To ensure Jane cannot disturb the rest of the household while they finish their evening activities.
options.B: To show that Jane is being imprisoned and has absolutely no power over her own situation.
options.C: To make Jane feel the same fear that John Reed felt when he was locked in that room as punishment.
options.D: To teach Jane that her emotional outbursts have serious and lasting consequences.

questions.explanationHtml:
Locking a child in a room — especially a dead person's former chamber — shows imprisonment and complete lack of power. It goes beyond normal discipline to total control.

A is possible but too narrow; the detail is symbolic, not just practical. C has no textual evidence. D is a reasonable surface reading, but the passage emphasizes powerlessness, not just consequences.

questions.questionHtml: Which detail from the passage BEST supports the idea that Jane feels completely powerless in the Reed household?

options.A: "I resisted all the way"
options.B: "less than a servant"
options.C: "I will not stir"
options.D: "locked it behind them"

questions.explanationHtml: Locking the door removes all agency from Jane. She cannot leave, cannot argue, cannot act. While other options show conflict or status, only the locked door physically and symbolically confirms total powerlessness.

questions.questionHtml: What tone does the author create by having Miss Abbot say that "something bad might be permitted to come down the chimney and fetch you away"?

options.A: A playful, teasing tone meant to scare Jane lightly
options.B: A serious, religious tone about the dangers of sin
options.C: A harsh, intimidating tone that mixes superstition with control
options.D: A protective tone, warning Jane for her own safety

questions.explanationHtml:
The phrasing is deliberately vague ("something bad") and superstitious ("come down the chimney"), combined with religious threat ("God will punish her"). The tone is harsh and meant to frighten, not to protect or play.

A is incorrect; it's not playful. B is too narrow — it's not purely religious; it's superstitious and controlling. D is incorrect; there is no warmth or genuine concern here.

questions.questionHtml:
Place the following events in the order they occur in the passage. Which of the following sequences is correct?

Events:
A. Bessie warns Jane that if she does not sit still, she must be tied down, and she asks Miss Abbot for her garters.
B. Jane cries out, "Don't take them off; I will not stir."
C. Miss Abbot tells Jane, "No; you are less than a servant, for you do nothing for your keep."
D. Miss Abbot warns that God might strike Jane dead and that "something bad" might come down the chimney.
E. Jane asks, "Master! How is he my master? Am I a servant?"

options.A: E, C, A, B, D
options.B: E, A, C, B, D
options.C: C, E, A, B, D
options.D: A, C, E, B, D

questions.explanationHtml:
The correct chronological order:
1. Jane asks, "Am I a servant?" (E)
2. Miss Abbot replies, "No; you are less than a servant..." (C)
3. Bessie threatens to tie her down and asks for garters (A)
4. Jane cries out, "Don't take them off; I will not stir" (B)
5. Miss Abbot gives the supernatural warning before they leave and lock the door (D)

questions.questionHtml:
Place the following events in the order they occur in the passage. Which of the following sequences is correct?

Events:
A. The convict eats the bread ravenously while Pip sits trembling on a tombstone.
B. The convict seizes Pip by the chin, his teeth chattering.
C. The convict turns Pip upside down and empties his pockets.
D. The convict demands, "Tell us your name!" and Pip answers, "Pip. Pip, sir."
E. Pip points to his village after the convict demands to know where he lives.

options.A: B, D, E, C, A
options.B: D, B, E, C, A
options.C: B, E, D, C, A
options.D: B, D, C, E, A

questions.explanationHtml: The correct chronological order is: 1. The convict seizes Pip by the chin (B). 2. He demands Pip's name, and Pip answers (D). 3. Pip points to his village (E). 4. The convict turns Pip upside down and empties his pockets (C). 5. Only after gaining full compliance does the convict eat the bread ravenously (A). This sequence shows the convict's method: physical intimidation, information gathering, search, and finally food.

questions.questionHtml: How does the description of the churchyard, marshes, river, and sea affect the reader's understanding of Pip's situation?

options.A: It shows that Pip lives in a beautiful, peaceful place and is therefore safe.
options.B: It creates a gloomy, threatening atmosphere that makes Pip's fear feel natural and overwhelming.
options.C: It contrasts sharply with Pip's happy memories of his parents.
options.D: It proves that the convict chose this location because he knew the cattle would protect him.

questions.explanationHtml: Words like "bleak," "dark flat wilderness," "savage lair," and "low leaden line" build a frightening mood that matches Pip's terror. The setting is not beautiful or peaceful (A); there are no happy memories of parents (C); and the cattle are merely described as "scattered," not as protectors (D). The gloomy atmosphere makes Pip's fear feel natural and overwhelming.

questions.questionHtml: Based on the passage, which statement best describes the convict's behavior toward Pip?

options.A: He treats Pip as an equal and asks politely for help.
options.B: He uses physical threats and intimidation to frighten Pip into obedience.
options.C: He ignores Pip completely and only talks to himself.
options.D: He tries to befriend Pip by sharing the bread and telling stories.

questions.explanationHtml: The convict threatens to cut Pip's throat, growls, seizes him by the chin, and his terrifying appearance alone controls Pip. There is no politeness (A), no ignoring (C), and no friendship or sharing (D). His behavior is consistently threatening and intimidating.

questions.questionHtml: The passage says Pip derived his beliefs about his parents and brothers "unreasonably" from tombstones. What does this word choice suggest about Pip's thinking?

options.A: Pip is intentionally lying about his family to make himself seem more interesting.
options.B: Pip is too young to understand death, so his conclusions are childlike and imaginative, not logical.
options.C: Pip has been told the truth by his sister but refuses to believe her.
options.D: The tombstones actually contain detailed descriptions that Pip misreads.

questions.explanationHtml: Pip thinks his father was "square, stout, dark" because of the shape of letters on a tombstone, and that his brothers were born with hands in pockets because of the stone lozenges' shape. "Unreasonably" highlights childish fantasy, not malice or deception. There is no lying (A), no refusal to believe his sister (C), and the tombstones have no detailed descriptions (D).

questions.questionHtml: The convict is described as having "a great iron on his leg." What does this detail most likely imply about him?

options.A: He is a blacksmith like Joe Gargery and carries tools for work.
options.B: He is an escaped prisoner who has broken free from leg irons.
options.C: He is a sailor who wears iron weights to stay steady on a ship.
options.D: He is a grave digger who uses the iron to mark burial plots.

questions.explanationHtml: An "iron on his leg" (a shackle) is a classic detail of an escaped convict. His wet, muddy, torn condition matches someone who has fled through marshes. There is no evidence he is a blacksmith (A), sailor (C), or grave digger (D).

questions.questionHtml: Which action in the passage best proves that the convict prioritizes control over food?

options.A: He tells Pip to "Keep still" before asking his name.
options.B: He eats the bread only after he has questioned, searched, and frightened Pip.
options.C: He turns Pip upside down to empty his pockets.
options.D: He shivers and has broken shoes.

questions.explanationHtml: Despite being hungry enough to eat "ravenously," the convict delays eating until he has questioned Pip, searched his pockets, and fully intimidated him. This proves control is his first priority. Options A and C are part of the control sequence but do not directly show the prioritization over food. Option D describes his condition but does not relate to control over food.

questions.questionHtml: What can be inferred about who raises Pip?

options.A: Pip lives alone in the churchyard because all his relatives are dead.
options.B: Pip's mother is still alive but too sick to care for him.
options.C: Pip's sister (Mrs. Joe Gargery) and her husband the blacksmith are his guardians.
options.D: Pip was adopted by the village priest after his parents died.

questions.explanationHtml: The passage says Pip gives his father's name "on the authority of his tombstone and my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith." Both parents and five brothers are dead, so his sister is the surviving relative who raises him. Pip does not live alone (A), his mother is dead (B), and there is no mention of a village priest (D).

questions.questionHtml: After Miss Watson describes the "bad place," Huck says he wishes he were there. What does his reaction most likely reveal about his character?

options.A: He is genuinely evil and wants to be punished for his behavior.
options.B: He is bored and frustrated with his current life, not actually wicked.
options.C: He believes the "bad place" is the same as the adventure Tom Sawyer promised.
options.D: He wants to frighten Miss Watson into leaving him alone.

questions.explanationHtml:
The passage shows Huck is restless, "cramped," "deadly dull," and "fidgety." He explicitly says, "All I wanted was to go somewheres; all I wanted was a change, I warn't particular." His comment is impulsive frustration, not genuine evil. Option B captures his true motive: boredom, not wickedness.

A is wrong because Huck shows no real malice. C is wrong because there is no link to Tom's adventures here. D is wrong because he isn't trying to scare her; he speaks carelessly.

questions.questionHtml: Huck compares the widow's way of cooking (everything cooked "by itself") to a "barrel of odds and ends" where things mix and juices swap around. What does this comparison most directly show about Huck's attitude toward the widow's rules?

options.A: He thinks the widow's cooking tastes bad because she uses the wrong ingredients.
options.B: He prefers the widow's orderly method because it keeps foods separate and clean.
options.C: He dislikes the widow's rigid, separate way of doing things and prefers a looser, more natural mix.
options.D: He is confused about how to cook because he never learned proper meal preparation.

questions.explanationHtml:
Huck clearly prefers the barrel where things mix together ("things go better"). The widow's rule of keeping every food separate feels cramped to him, just like her other rules (sitting straight, no smoking, praying before meals). This comparison directly shows he dislikes her rigid, separate way of doing things.

A is wrong because he never says the food tastes bad; he objects to the method. B is wrong because he does not prefer order and separation. D is wrong because this is about preference, not confusion or lack of knowledge.

questions.questionHtml: Why does Huck decide not to tell Miss Watson that he won't try to go to the "good place"?

options.A: He is afraid she will physically punish him if he disagrees.
options.B: He secretly hopes to go there but doesn't want to admit it.
options.C: He thinks arguing is pointless and would only create conflict without helping anyone.
options.D: He plans to run away that night, so he sees no reason to respond.

questions.explanationHtml:
Huck's exact words: "I never said so, because it would only make trouble, and wouldn't do no good." He has already seen Miss Watson get angry. He learns that telling her his real opinion leads to arguments and no change. Option C matches his pragmatic, avoidant reasoning.

A is wrong because the text shows no fear of physical punishment; he just avoids "trouble." B is wrong because he clearly sees "no advantage" in her good place. D is wrong because his escape happens later at midnight; this decision comes earlier, and he doesn't mention running away as the reason.

questions.questionHtml:
Place the following events in the order they occur in the passage. Which of the following sequences is correct?

Events:
A. Huck says he wishes he were in the "bad place" after Miss Watson describes it.
B. Huck hears a twig snap in the dark among the trees, then a soft "me-yow."
C. The widow takes out her book and teaches Huck about Moses and the Bulrushers.
D. Miss Watson tells Huck to sit up straight and not to scrunch or gap.
E. Huck puts out the light, scrambles out the window, and meets Tom Sawyer in the trees.

options.A: C, D, A, B, E
options.B: C, A, D, B, E
options.C: D, C, A, B, E
options.D: A, B, C, D, E

questions.explanationHtml:
The correct chronological order is: 1. The widow teaches about Moses (C). 2. Miss Watson gives commands to sit straight, not scrunch, not gap (D). 3. After those commands, Miss Watson describes the bad place, and Huck says he wishes he were there (A). 4. After midnight, Huck hears a twig snap and the "me-yow" signal (B). 5. Huck puts out the light, climbs out, and meets Tom (E).

Option A correctly lists C, D, A, B, E. The other options misplace events: B puts A before D, C starts with D instead of C, and D starts with A.
